6. Review app security, share, and manage

Designing an app with AppSheet is an iterative process [1] that generally follows a core framework to build, customize, and deploy your solution [2]. Here are the six primary steps every app creator should follow:
1. Define your entities

2. Build your spreadsheet
If you are starting with existing data, you should structure it in a supported platform like Google Sheets, Microsoft Excel, or Smartsheet [5, 6]. Every defined entity must have its own dedicated worksheet, where the properties are laid out as the column headers [5, 7].

Alternatively, if you are not starting from an existing spreadsheet, you can create your app by starting with a blank app, using a pre-built template, or describing your idea using natural language to Gemini in AppSheet for an AI-assisted build [2, 6, 8].
3. Plug in your spreadsheet
4. Define the user experience (UX)
5. Refine the app behavior
Static configuration: Fixed, simple settings applied to all users, such as making a column read-only or defining offline behavior rules [14, 15].
Dynamic configuration: Creating tailored behaviors using spreadsheet-like expressions (formulas) to dynamically hide columns, format data, or compute virtual columns [15-18].

Actions: Custom buttons and operations that execute specific logical steps for the user, such as updating a record's status, navigating to a different view, or opening an external application [13, 19].
Automation: Using bots to trigger complex tasks behind the scenes—like sending emails, creating push notifications, or parsing documents—based on data changes or recurring time schedules [20-22].
2. Build Your Spreadsheet

AppSheet apps are fundamentally driven by data. You must first categorize your data into entities (representing real-world things like employees, jobs, or customers) and their properties (details like names, addresses, or phone numbers) [3, 4]. Every instance of an entity shares the same properties but holds unique values, and you must also define how these entities are related to one another [4, 5].
To integrate your data into your app, simply navigate to the Data panel in the AppSheet editor, click +, and select the specific spreadsheet or data tables you want to connect [7].

The UX definition determines what your users see and how they interact with the interface [9, 10]. You visualize data by configuring different Views, such as calendars, maps, detail lists, or dashboards [9]. To capture new information from users, you rely on Form views, which AppSheet automatically generates for any table that permits data additions or updates [11, 12].

While AppSheet provides default capabilities for data syncing and form editing, you can heavily customize your app's functionality [12, 13]. You can refine behavior using four increasingly powerful approaches [14]:

Before distributing your app, you must secure it [23]. In most business environments, you will restrict access by requiring users to sign in and explicitly whitelisting their email addresses [24, 25]. You can also apply dynamic row-level security filters so that different users only see the data specifically relevant to them [26]. Once secured and shared, you can utilize AppSheet's management tools to track app performance, collaborate with your team, manage version control, and troubleshoot errors as you continue to iterate on your design [1, 27].

Quick Reference Checklist
Account & Licensing
AppSheet Account: You'll need an active AppSheet account. Consider your team's subscription tier, as different plans offer varying features and user limits.
Workspace Access: Ensure all team members have appropriate access levels and permissions configured.
API Keys: Generate and securely store API keys if you plan to integrate with external systems.
Data Source Requirements
Data Format: Prepare your data in a compatible format (Google Sheets, Microsoft Excel, SQL databases, or Salesforce). AppSheet works best when data is well-organized before import.
Data Cleanup: Remove duplicates, standardize field names, and validate data integrity before connecting to AppSheet.
Backup: Always maintain a backup of your original data source before making structural changes.
Permissions: Ensure you have read and write access to the data source, and that AppSheet has proper credentials to connect.
Team Structure & Roles
Designer/Developer: The primary person building the app (you, likely).
Business Owner: Stakeholder who defines requirements and validates the app meets business needs.
End Users: People who will eventually use the app—involve them early for feedback.
Administrator: Manages security, user access, and deployment settings.
Planning & Requirements
Define Goals: What problem does this app solve? What are the success metrics?
User Workflows: Document how different user roles will interact with the app.
Feature List: Create a prioritized list of "must-have" vs. "nice-to-have" features.
Timeline: Set realistic milestones for design, testing, and deployment.
Technical Considerations
Device Requirements: Will users access via mobile, desktop, or both? This affects UI/UX decisions.
Connectivity: Does your app need to work offline? Plan accordingly.
Integration Needs: Identify external systems you need to connect to (CRM, email, payment systems, etc.).
Security & Compliance: Understand any regulatory requirements (GDPR, HIPAA, etc.) that impact your design.
Data Modeling
Normalize Your Data: Keep related information organized. Avoid redundant data across entities—use relationships instead.
Clear Naming Conventions: Use consistent, descriptive names for entities and properties. Future developers (including yourself) will thank you.
Unique Identifiers: Each entity should have a primary key that uniquely identifies each record (e.g., ID, Email, SKU).
Document Relationships: Clearly define how entities relate to each other—one-to-many, many-to-many, etc.
User Experience (UX) Design
Keep It Simple: Start with the core workflow. Features can always be added later.
Mobile-First Approach: Design for mobile users first, then enhance for desktop. Mobile constraints force clarity.
Consistent Navigation: Make it easy for users to move between screens. Use predictable patterns.
Clear Feedback: Show users what their actions accomplished. Use confirmations, success messages, and error alerts appropriately.
Development Workflow
Iterate in Stages: Build a Minimum Viable Product (MVP) first. Get user feedback before adding advanced features.
Test Early & Often: Don't wait until the end to test. Involve users in testing at each stage.
Document as You Go: Keep notes on design decisions and configurations. This helps when you need to make changes later.
Use Environments: Set up separate development and production environments to avoid breaking live apps.
Performance & Scalability
Optimize Queries: Minimize data pulls. Use filtering and sorting to reduce the amount of data processed.
Limit Initial Load: Don't load all data at once. Use pagination or lazy loading for large datasets.
Cache Data When Possible: For offline capability and performance, cache essential data locally on devices.
Security & Governance
Role-Based Access: Define different user roles with appropriate permissions. Not everyone needs to see or edit everything.
Audit Trails: Track who did what and when. This is critical for compliance and troubleshooting.
Data Validation: Validate all data inputs to prevent errors and malicious data entry.
Secure Credentials: Never hardcode passwords or API keys. Use secure storage mechanisms.
Collaboration & Communication
Regular Check-Ins: Keep stakeholders updated on progress. Catch issues early.
Gather Feedback: Involve end users throughout the process, not just at the end.
Document Requirements: Write down what the app should do and get buy-in from stakeholders before building.
Planning & Scope Creep
Skipping the Planning Phase: Jumping straight into building without clear requirements leads to rework and delays.
Unlimited Feature Requests: Define scope upfront and manage changes carefully. Every new feature adds complexity.
Ignoring User Input: Building what you think users need, not what they actually need, results in unused features.
Data & Integration Issues
Dirty Data: Importing messy, unvalidated data causes problems downstream. Clean your data first.
Poor Data Structure: Denormalizing data or creating overly complex relationships makes the app hard to maintain.
Incomplete Integration Testing: Don't assume integrations work until you've thoroughly tested them with real data.
Mismatched Field Types: Using text fields for dates or numbers causes validation and calculation errors.
User Experience Mistakes
Overcomplicating Interfaces: Cramming too many features into one screen overwhelms users. Prioritize the primary workflow.
Poor Navigation: Users shouldn't need a map to find features. Keep navigation intuitive and consistent.
Missing Error Handling: Users don't know what went wrong when something breaks. Provide clear, actionable error messages.
Ignoring Mobile Experience: Assuming a desktop app will translate to mobile without redesign is a common failure.
Technical & Performance
Not Testing Performance: An app that works perfectly with 100 records may fail with 10,000. Test with realistic data volumes.
Inefficient Queries: Pulling all data and filtering in the app instead of at the source is slow and wasteful.
Neglecting Offline Scenarios: If offline capability is needed, don't design it as an afterthought—build it in from the start.
Security & Compliance
Weak Access Controls: Giving all users the same permissions is a security and data privacy risk.
Exposing Sensitive Data: Logging sensitive information or displaying it unnecessarily creates compliance issues.
No Audit Trail: Without tracking who accessed or changed what, you can't investigate issues or prove compliance.
Deployment & Maintenance
Testing Only With Happy Path: Focus on edge cases and error scenarios, not just the ideal flow.
Deploying Without a Rollback Plan: If something breaks in production, you need a way to quickly revert.
Insufficient User Training: Releasing an app without proper training leads to confusion and misuse.
No Backup Strategy: Always have a backup before making major changes to production data.
Example 1: Inventory Management App
Business Problem: A retail company needs to track inventory across multiple locations in real-time.
Entities: Products, Locations, Inventory (stock levels), Suppliers, Transactions (additions/removals)
Key Features: Low stock alerts, transfer between locations, barcode scanning, audit trail of all changes.
Challenges Solved: Synced data across locations, offline operation for scanning, role-based permissions (warehouse staff vs. managers).
Success Metrics: 30% reduction in stockouts, faster inventory counts, improved accuracy.
Example 2: Field Service Application
Business Problem: Service technicians need to track jobs, capture photos, and log time in the field without constant connectivity.
Entities: Customers, Service Requests, Technicians, Work Orders, Time Tracking, Photo Attachments
Key Features: Job assignment, offline data sync, photo/signature capture, time tracking, customer communication, invoice generation.
Challenges Solved: Offline capability, map-based job routing, automatic sync when reconnected, real-time dispatch updates.
Success Metrics: 40% improvement in job completion time, 95% data capture accuracy, reduced administrative overhead.
Example 3: Employee Onboarding Portal
Business Problem: HR needs to streamline the onboarding process with document collection, training assignments, and manager approvals.
Entities: Employees, Onboarding Tasks, Documents, Training Modules, Approvals, Departments
Key Features: Multi-step workflow with approvals, document uploads, training completion tracking, progress dashboards, email notifications.
Challenges Solved: Automated workflow routing, conditional task assignment, document version control, audit trail for compliance.
Success Metrics: 50% faster onboarding, 100% document capture, improved employee satisfaction scores.
Key Takeaways From These Examples
Start Simple: Each app began with core entities and essential features, then added complexity based on user feedback.
Mobile-First Design: All three examples required offline capability and mobile optimization—don't skip this.
Workflow Automation: Apps that automate repetitive tasks deliver the most business value.
Role-Based Access: Different user types need different views and capabilities. Plan this from the start.
Integration Matters: Real-world apps rarely exist in isolation. Integration with email, CRM, or ERP systems is often essential.
Automations & Workflows
Workflow Automation: Use AppSheet automations to trigger actions based on data changes (e.g., send an email when a task is marked complete).
Process Flows: Define multi-step processes that move data through statuses and route to appropriate users.
Scheduled Tasks: Run automations on a schedule (daily, weekly) for routine operations like data synchronization or report generation.
Conditional Logic: Use expressions to make automations context-aware. Only trigger actions when specific conditions are met.
Custom Expressions & Formulas
Calculated Fields: Use expressions to compute values dynamically (e.g., total = unit price × quantity).
Text Functions: Concatenate fields, extract substrings, or format text for display purposes.
Date Functions: Calculate time differences, add days, or format dates for reports.
Conditional Expressions: Use IF statements to show/hide fields or change validation rules based on data.
API Integrations
REST APIs: Connect to external services to fetch or send data. Examples: weather data, payment processing, CRM systems.
Webhook Integrations: Set up webhooks to receive real-time notifications when data changes in external systems.
Authentication: Handle OAuth, API keys, and other authentication methods securely.
Error Handling: Test integrations thoroughly and implement fallbacks for when external APIs are unavailable.
Multi-User Synchronization
Data Sync Strategy: Plan how data will sync across devices and users. Understand conflict resolution (last-write-wins, user preference, etc.).
Offline-First Architecture: Design the app to work offline with data syncing when connectivity returns.
Bandwidth Optimization: Use selective sync and compression to minimize bandwidth usage, especially important for mobile users.
Advanced Security
Row-Level Security: Control which rows users can see based on their role or relationship to the data (e.g., salespeople only see their own leads).
Column-Level Access: Hide sensitive columns from certain users (e.g., salary info visible only to HR).
Encryption: Encrypt sensitive data both in transit and at rest.
Two-Factor Authentication: Add extra security for sensitive apps or user roles.
Performance Optimization
Index Key Columns: Mark frequently searched or filtered columns as keys to improve performance.
Lazy Loading: Load data on-demand rather than all at once.
Caching Strategies: Cache reference data locally to reduce server calls.
Query Optimization: Write efficient filters and sorting rules to minimize data transferred.
Analytics & Reporting
Dashboard Creation: Build dashboards that summarize key metrics and KPIs for business users.
Export Capabilities: Allow users to export data to Excel or PDF for further analysis.
Business Intelligence: Integrate with BI tools for advanced analytics and data visualization.
General Questions
Q: How long does it take to build an AppSheet app?

A: A simple app can be built in days, while complex apps with integrations may take weeks or months. The time depends on data complexity, feature scope, and team experience. A well-planned MVP typically takes 2-4 weeks.
Q: Do I need coding experience to use AppSheet?
A: No. AppSheet is designed for low-code/no-code development. However, understanding basic logic and workflows helps. For complex integrations, some technical knowledge is beneficial.
Q: Can I build an app without a predefined data source?
A: Yes, but it's not ideal. AppSheet works best when you start with a well-structured data source. You can create sheets or databases within AppSheet, but defining structure upfront is better.
Data & Integration Issues
Q: My data won't sync. What should I check?

A: Check: (1) Data source credentials and permissions, (2) Network connectivity, (3) Data format compliance with AppSheet requirements, (4) Any data validation errors in the source, (5) AppSheet logs for specific error messages.
Q: Can I use multiple data sources in one app?
A: Yes. You can connect to different databases, spreadsheets, or services. Set up relationships between them if needed, but be aware of performance implications with too many sources.
Q: How do I handle large datasets efficiently?
A: Use pagination, filtering at the source (not in-app), lazy loading, and selective sync. Avoid loading all data upfront. Use indexed searches and consider archiving old data.
User Interface & Experience
Q: Can I customize the app's look and feel?
A: Yes, extensively. AppSheet offers themes, color schemes, fonts, and custom layouts. You can also create custom views tailored to different user roles.
Q: Why does my app feel slow on mobile?

A: Common causes: (1) Large images not optimized, (2) Too many fields loading simultaneously, (3) Complex calculations running on every record, (4) Poor network connection, (5) Unoptimized queries. Profile and optimize the slowest operations first.
Q: How do I make my app work offline?
A: Configure offline settings in AppSheet, set which tables sync locally, and use the offline-first development pattern. Test extensively offline and during sync scenarios.
Security & Access Control
Q: How do I prevent unauthorized data access?
A: Use row-level security (RLS) and column-level security (CLS). Set up role-based access controls. Use the UserId() or UserEmail() functions to filter data dynamically.
Q: Can I audit who changed what data and when?
A: Yes, AppSheet maintains audit logs. Enable detailed logging for sensitive data. You can also create custom audit trails by tracking changes with automations.
Q: Is my data encrypted?

A: AppSheet encrypts data in transit (HTTPS). For at-rest encryption, it depends on your data source (Google Drive, Salesforce, SQL, etc.). Check with your data provider or use client-side encryption for extra security.
Troubleshooting Common Problems
Problem: "Connection Failed" error when starting the app
Check: Network connectivity, data source availability, API keys and credentials, firewall rules blocking AppSheet services, data source permissions.
Problem: Data doesn't update across devices
Check: Sync settings enabled, network connectivity, data source supports real-time sync, no conflicting edits happening simultaneously, offline cache cleared when needed.
Problem: App crashes or freezes when loading data
Check: Data volume (too many records?), complex calculations slowing things down, images or media files too large, RAM limitations on device, queries that take too long to execute.
Problem: Users seeing data they shouldn't have access to
Check: Row-level security rules configured correctly, column-level access applied, role definitions accurate, UserId() or UserEmail() functions working as expected, test with actual user accounts.
Problem: Automated workflows not triggering
Check: Workflow conditions match your intent, data actually meets the conditions, automation is enabled, check logs for error messages, test manually first to verify logic.
User Monitoring & Support
Track Usage Metrics: Monitor which features users actually use. High adoption of a feature means it's solving a real problem.
Set Up Error Tracking: Monitor app crashes and errors. Use error logs to identify and fix issues quickly.
Collect User Feedback: Use surveys, in-app feedback, or direct conversations to understand pain points and feature requests.
Respond to Support Issues Quickly: Establish SLAs for response times. Quick support reduces frustration and increases adoption.
Performance Monitoring
Monitor Load Times: Track how long key operations take. If something slows down, investigate and optimize.
Database Performance: Monitor query times and identify slow queries. Optimize them or add indexes as needed.
Sync Performance: Track sync times and data transfer volumes. Optimize if sync becomes slow or bandwidth-heavy.
Device Performance: Test on various devices and network conditions. Not all devices are equal.
Data Quality & Maintenance
Data Validation: Regularly check data for inconsistencies, duplicates, or errors. Set up automated validation rules.
Backup & Recovery: Ensure backups run regularly. Test restore procedures before you need them in an emergency.
Data Cleanup: Archive old data periodically to keep the database performant and reduce storage costs.
Document Data Changes: Keep records of schema changes, migrations, or data transformations for troubleshooting.
Version Management & Updates
Version Control: Maintain different versions of your app for development, testing, and production. Never make changes directly in production.
Change Log: Document all changes, bug fixes, and new features. Users appreciate knowing what's new.
Staged Rollouts: Deploy new features to a subset of users first. Monitor for issues before rolling out to everyone.
Rollback Plan: Have a plan to quickly revert to the previous version if a new release causes problems.
Feature Iteration & Improvements
Prioritize Feature Requests: Use data and feedback to decide what to build next. Not every request is worth implementing.
A/B Testing: Test different approaches with different user groups to see what works best.
Deprecate Old Features: If a feature is unused, consider removing it to reduce complexity. Communicate deprecation clearly.
Iterate Based on Feedback: The first version is rarely perfect. Plan for ongoing improvements based on real-world usage.
Security & Compliance Ongoing
Regular Security Audits: Periodically review access controls, permissions, and data exposure.
Compliance Checks: Ensure your app continues to meet regulatory requirements (GDPR, HIPAA, etc.).
Password & Key Rotation: Refresh API keys and credentials on a regular schedule.
Penetration Testing: For high-risk apps, conduct security testing to identify vulnerabilities.
Team & Documentation
Keep Docs Updated: As the app changes, update documentation and user guides. Out-of-date docs hurt adoption.
Train New Users: As new people join, provide training. A well-trained user base makes support easier.
Knowledge Transfer: Document design decisions and complex configurations. If you leave, the next person should be able to maintain the app.
Regular Review Meetings: Schedule periodic reviews with stakeholders to discuss usage, issues, and future direction.
